public_rationale: The qualified claim is supported. The contemporaneous announcement linked dismissal to deficient candor, and a director who voted for removal later explicitly attributed the loss of trust to alleged deception. These records reasonably support the appearance Marcus described. The subsequent review questioned the process and whether removal was warranted, but did not establish that dishonesty concerns played no role. This assessment does not convert 'appeared' into a finding that every alleged lie was proven. See the [board announcement](https://openai.com/index/openai-announces-leadership-transition/) and [Toner interview](https://www.ted.com/podcasts/the-ted-ai-show/what-really-went-down-at-openai-and-the-future-of-regulation-w-helen-toner).
limitations: The result depends on preserving the qualification and reading the claim as concerning the board's motivation.
Toner was a participant defending a disputed decision; her account is not an independent adjudication.
OpenAI's investigation disclosure is a company-published summary.
The cited Hagey excerpt was inaccessible.

public_payload.normalized_proposition: Sam Altman appears to have been fired from OpenAI in 2023 for lying.

statement.excerpt: Sam Altman does in fact appeared to have gotten fired in 2023 for lying, exactly as I speculated back when he was fired, in my essay “not consistently candid”.
statement.document_title: Scaling is over, the bubble may be deflating, LLMs still can’t reason, and you can’t trust Sam

our_interpretation: Preserve the qualification: assess whether the record reasonably supports the appearance that perceived dishonesty motivated Altman's dismissal, not whether every allegation of lying is conclusively established.
Read 'for lying' as describing the dismissing board's reason. It need not have been the sole reason.
The target period is 2023, the year explicitly named. Later accounts can provide evidence about that dismissal.
The comparison with Marcus's earlier speculation is not a separate claim being graded.
criteria.support_condition: Contemporaneous board statements and credible firsthand accounts reasonably support perceived dishonesty as a material reason for the 2023 dismissal. They need not conclusively establish the underlying allegations.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Reliable evidence establishes that perceived dishonesty was not a material reason for the dismissal, or discredits the accounts sufficiently that the qualified appearance is no longer reasonably supported. Disagreement about whether dismissal was justified is insufficient by itself.

evidence.explanation: The announcement connects dismissal to the board's finding that Altman's communications lacked consistent candor and hindered oversight. This supports an apparent dishonesty-related motive, while not independently proving deliberate lies.

evidence.locator: Helen Toner's answer beginning at 00:05:12; explanation continues at 00:07:09
evidence.explanation: This is firsthand testimony within a published interview. Explaining the November dismissal, Toner alleges deception and says the four dismissing directors concluded they could not believe Altman's statements.

evidence.locator: Summary of WilmerHale review & findings, paragraph beginning 'WilmerHale reviewed the public post'
evidence.explanation: The summary says the original announcement accurately reflected the board's reasons. However, it also says the board proceeded without a full inquiry or opportunity for Altman to respond, and that his conduct did not require removal; these findings limit any stronger conclusion that proven lies justified dismissal.
